617.title: The pull home
617.hook: Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, homesick for his bride
617.howItsDone: Nanda's story is often told in Buddhist communities, and in the Anguttara Nikaya Nanda is named foremost among monks in guarding the senses, the discipline he came to after his struggle.

segments.voice: Yesterday: piya, dear, and the king and queen on the palace roof. Your line: everyone loves themselves. Today, a monk who can't stop thinking about home.

First semester away. The new place is supposed to be the start of everything, and the student lying awake can only think about the kitchen at home, the dog, someone's voice saying come back soon. Nanda had his own version of that. He was the Buddha's half-brother, the son of Mahapajapati, and he had become a monk. But one day he tells the other monks: I'm not happy living this life. I can't keep it up. I'm going to give up the training and go back. Why? Because of a girl.
screen: `FIRST SEMESTER AWAY.` → `NANDA, THE HALF-BROTHER.` → `I CAN'T KEEP IT UP.`

segments.voice: When I left home, Nanda tells the Buddha, a Sakyan girl, the loveliest in the land, looked up at me with her hair half combed and said: come back soon, master. I keep remembering it. What the Buddha does next is startling. He takes Nanda by the arm and, the text says, as easily as a strong man bends his arm, the two vanish and appear in the heaven of the Thirty-Three. There Nanda sees five hundred heavenly nymphs. Which is lovelier, the Buddha asks, the Sakyan girl or these? Next to these, Nanda says, she's nothing at all. Then practice, the Buddha says, and I promise you these. So Nanda practices. But the other monks hear about the deal and tease him: Nanda the hired hand, Nanda working for wages. Ashamed, Nanda goes off alone and practices in earnest. And somewhere in that practice, the wanting itself falls away, both the girl and the nymphs. He goes back to the Buddha and says: I release you from your promise. I already knew, the Buddha says. The verse praises one who has crossed the mud of sense-desire and is no longer shaken by pleasure or pain. Some readers take the story as a bigger desire used to loosen a smaller one, until both drop away. And the ending is plain in the text: the pull wasn't beaten by force. It simply stopped pulling.

segments.voice: Ask gently what tugs at you when you try to keep a good intention: a habit, a person, a comfort, a picture in your head. Let it come, the way Nanda's memory came, and without fighting it or following it, feel where the pull lives in the body. Then rest with the breath, and notice that the pull, too, rises and fades.
Nanda. The Buddha's half-brother, homesick for the girl he left, until the wanting itself fell away.
Your line: it simply stopped pulling. Wanting rises and falls, like the breath. See you on day six hundred eighteen.

618.title: Not yet ripe
618.hook: Meghiya insists on going alone and is overwhelmed; five things ripen the mind
618.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the Meghiya Sutta to explain why practice is done with a teacher and a community, and the five supports it lists are taught across Theravada monastic life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nanda, the monk pulled toward home, until the pull fell away. Your line: it simply stopped pulling. Today, a monk who wants to go too fast.

Meghiya is serving as the Buddha's attendant. One morning, coming back from alms in a village, he walks along a river and finds a mango grove so lovely he can hardly stand it. Quiet, shady, by the water. The perfect place to meditate, he thinks. He hurries back and asks permission to go and sit there. Wait, the Buddha says. We're alone here. Stay until another monk comes. Meghiya asks again. Wait. A third time. And this time the Buddha says: what can I say, when you speak of striving? Go, Meghiya.
screen: `A MANGO GROVE BY THE RIVER.` → `WAIT UNTIL ANOTHER COMES.` → `WHAT CAN I SAY? GO.`

segments.voice: Meghiya goes and sits under a mango tree in the perfect grove. And there, in the perfect place, his mind is overrun. Three kinds of thought keep coming at him: thoughts of sense-pleasure, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harming. He's amazed: I went forth out of faith, and here I am, swarmed by these. He comes back and tells the Buddha everything. The Buddha doesn't say I told you so. He says that when the mind's release is not yet ripe, five things bring it to ripeness. First, a good friend, a good companion. Second, keeping the training, living with integrity. Third, talk that actually helps: about wanting little, contentment, solitude, energy, wisdom. Fourth, effort, letting go of what's unskillful and taking up what's skillful. Fifth, wisdom that sees how things rise and pass. And notice which comes first. The good friend: the very thing Meghiya walked away from when he left the Buddha alone to sit in his beautiful grove. Then the Buddha adds what to do with the thoughts: reflect on the body's unattractiveness to ease lust, kindness to ease ill will, mindfulness of breathing to cut the chatter, and seeing impermanence to uproot the conceit I am. The place wasn't the problem. Meghiya wasn't ready yet, and the Buddha could see it. Ripeness can't be rushed.

Let yourself hear it again without defending against it, and ask whether there's something here you're not ripe enough to see yet. You don't have to decide anything; just let it be heard, and rest with the breath.

619.title: Each held a part
619.hook: the blind men and the elephant, read whole
619.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the elephant story when teaching about clinging to views, and versions of it are also told in Jain, Hindu and Sufi traditions, each with its own lesson.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Meghiya in the mango grove. Your line: a good friend comes first. Today, a story you've met before, read from its home in the Udana.

Water pot. Winnowing basket. Plowshare. Broom. Each blind man touches one part of the elephant and names it. You heard this story on day three hundred fifty-eight. It turns up on posters and in classrooms, and other traditions tell it too. But short retellings often keep only the middle, and drop how it starts and how it ends. Today we read it whole, from the sixth chapter of the Udana, and listen for three things the short version leaves out: who it was told to, the line about the king, and the verse.
screen: `WATER POT, BASKET, PLOWSHARE, BROOM.` → `SHORT VERSIONS KEEP THE MIDDLE.` → `TODAY, THE WHOLE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. The monks come back from town troubled. Teachers of many groups are arguing: is the world eternal or not, finite or not, is the soul the same as the body, does one who is awakened exist after death? And they're wounding each other, the text says, with mouths like daggers. So the story is told to monks, about a city full of argument. Second, the king. After the blind men fight with their fists, the text says simply that the king was delighted. Why? It doesn't explain. Some readers hear a man enjoying a spectacle he arranged; others hear the delight of someone who sees the whole while the others see parts. The text leaves it open. And notice something easy to miss: none of the men lied. The one at the ear really did feel a winnowing basket. Each report was true about its part. What went wrong was the word only. Third, the verse the Buddha speaks after the story. Some teachers and seekers, it says, are attached to these views. They quarrel and dispute, people who see just one side. The problem isn't seeing a part; everyone sees a part. The problem is clinging, and then fighting. Last time the lesson was: hear out a view you dislike. Today goes further: listen to the whole, before you judge.
screen: `MOUTHS LIKE DAGGERS.` · `THE KING WAS DELIGHTED.` · `NO ONE LIED; THE WORD WAS ONLY.` · `PEOPLE WHO SEE ONE SIDE.` · then, large: `EACH HELD A PART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent moment when you made up your mind about someone before they'd finished talking, and replay it slowly. What part were they holding, and what part were you, and is there a word only hiding in your own view? Don't argue it out; let both parts sit side by side, and breathe.
Ditthi, a view or opinion. In Udana 6.4, every blind man's report was true about his part; the quarrel came from clinging to one side. Today's word.

620.title: The moths and the lamp
620.hook: insects flying into the oil lamps at night
620.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers sometimes use the image of insects and a flame for craving that harms the one who craves, drawing on scenes like this one in the Udana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elephant, read whole. Your line: listen to the whole. Today, a scene in the Udana that's over in a few lines.

A porch light on a summer night. Moths come out of the dark, circle the bulb, bump it, drift off, circle again. A bulb is one thing. An open flame is another: a moth that flies into a candle or an oil lamp doesn't come out again. Why do they keep coming? The Udana doesn't try to explain the moths. It just watches them.
screen: `A PORCH LIGHT ON A SUMMER NIGHT.` → `A FLAME IS DIFFERENT.` → `THE UDANA JUST WATCHES.`

segments.voice: The whole story takes a few lines. The Buddha is sitting outdoors in the dark of the night, and oil lamps are burning. Winged insects are flying around them and falling in, one after another, to their harm, to their ruin. The Buddha sees this, and, knowing the meaning of it, speaks a verse. Rushing up, passing by what's essential, they bring on new bonds again and again, like insects falling into a lamp. So some are bound up in what is seen and heard. That's all. No crowd, no question, no long teaching. A man sitting in the dark, watching. Notice the phrase in the middle: passing by what's essential. The moths aren't stupid. They're drawn by something real, the light. The trouble is that they mistake it for something it isn't, and keep coming back. The verse says people can do the same with the seen and the heard: the bright thing on the screen, the voice that pulls at us, each rush tying another knot. There's a link back to Bahiya, a few days ago: in the seen, only the seen. The moth doesn't stop at the seen. It flies straight in. And the Buddha doesn't put out the lamps or explain the insects. He sits in the dark, sees them, and speaks about people.
screen: `OIL LAMPS BURNING IN THE DARK.` · `FALLING IN, ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `PASSING BY WHAT'S ESSENTIAL.` · `BOUND BY THE SEEN AND THE HEARD.` · then, large: `THE MOTHS AND THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what bright thing you keep circling, even when it burns a little: a feed, a fight, a craving, an evening that always ends the same way. Picture it as a lamp in the dark, and watch yourself circling it with kindness, the way the Buddha watched the moths. You don't have to stop yet; just see the circling.
Adhipataka, a moth. In the Udana, insects falling into oil lamps at night: the picture of rushing again and again to the seen and the heard. Today's word.
Your line: the moths and the flame. The light is real; the rushing is the trouble. See you tomorrow.

621.title: She still gave
621.hook: Suppavasa, in a long and hard pregnancy, still gives; she is safely delivered
621.tomorrow: A hundred dear, a hundred sorrows
621.howItsDone: In some Theravada communities families invite monks for a meal and a blessing around a birth, and protective chants are sometimes recited for women in childbirth.

segments.voice: Yesterday: insects falling into the lamps. Your line: the moths and the flame. Today, a woman in pain who still thinks of others.

A hospital waiting room. The coffee goes cold. The clock seems broken. Every time the door opens, every head looks up. The Udana tells of Suppavasa, a Koliyan noblewoman, whose wait the text measures in years. It says she carried her child for seven years, and was in labor for seven days. Readers take those numbers in different ways; what's plain is a very long, very hard wait. And in the middle of it, she does something unexpected.
screen: `A HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `SUPPAVASA, THE KOLIYAN.` → `A VERY LONG, VERY HARD WAIT.`

segments.voice: In her pain, the text says, Suppavasa holds on to three thoughts. The Buddha teaches the way out of suffering like this. His community practices that way. And there is a peace where suffering like this doesn't exist. The teacher, the community, the peace, held in labor. She sends her husband to bow at the Buddha's feet in her name and tell him how she is. The Buddha says: may Suppavasa be well and free from illness, and give birth to a healthy son. And at that moment, the text says, she does. Then the part the title is about. As soon as she's able, she sends her husband back to invite the Buddha and the monks for meals, seven days in a row. She has just come through seven days of labor, and her first wish is to give. The Buddha even asks her: would you want another child like this one? Yes, she says, she would have seven more. The verse that follows is surprising: what is unpleasant comes disguised as pleasant, the hateful as dear, pain in the form of happiness, and overwhelms the heedless. Readers take it in different ways; some hear the Buddha seeing her joy and her pain held together. Tradition says the child grew up to be the monk Sivali, remembered for how freely gifts came to him.
screen: `THREE THOUGHTS, HELD IN LABOR.` · `MAY SHE BE WELL.` · `SEVEN DAYS OF MEALS.` · `PAIN IN THE FORM OF HAPPINESS.` · then, large: `SHE STILL GAVE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who is in a long wait right now, for a baby, a diagnosis, a visa, a phone call, and picture them where they are. Wish them well, the way the Buddha wished Suppavasa well: may you be well and free from illness. Let the wish be quiet and plain, in your own words or none, and if you pray, hold them in your prayers.

622.title: A hundred dear, a hundred sorrows
622.hook: Visakha grieves a grandchild; how many would you want to love?
622.howItsDone: Visakha is honored in Theravada tradition as a model lay disciple, and teachers sometimes tell her story alongside Kisa Gotami's when speaking about grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Suppavasa. Your line: give one small thing anyway. Today, another woman, another child, and a much harder morning.

Visakha comes to the Buddha in the middle of the day, her clothes wet, her hair wet. A granddaughter she dearly loved has died. The text doesn't say why she's wet; some readers take it as the washing after a funeral. Visakha is a lay follower the early texts honor for her generosity; tradition says she built a monastery in Savatthi. Why have you come here at midday, the Buddha asks, with your clothes and hair wet? She tells him. And he answers with a question.
screen: `VISAKHA, THE GIVER.` → `WET CLOTHES AT MIDDAY.` → `HE ANSWERS WITH A QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Visakha, he asks, would you like to have as many children and grandchildren as there are people in Savatthi? Yes, she says. And how many people die in Savatthi each day? Ten, she says, or nine, or five, or one. Savatthi is never without someone dying. Then, he says, would you ever be without wet clothes and wet hair? No, she says. Enough with so many. Then the Buddha says it plainly: those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have ninety have ninety. And so on, down to one: one dear, one sorrow. Those who have none dear have no sorrow. Then the verse: grief and lamentation and all the many kinds of suffering in the world exist because of what is dear. Where there's nothing dear, they don't. You may remember Kisa Gotami from the first year, and not long ago, the dart of grief. This is the same teaching from another side. Notice how he does it. He doesn't tell Visakha her grief is a mistake. He lets her do the arithmetic herself. Buddhist teachers read the line in more than one way. Some say it's about clinging, holding the dear as mine, not about ceasing to love; the same canon praises boundless kindness to all. Others hear in it the monk's path of renunciation.
screen: `AS MANY AS LIVE IN SAVATTHI?` · `NEVER A DAY WITHOUT A DEATH.` · `ONE DEAR, ONE SORROW.` · `SHE DOES THE ARITHMETIC.` · then, large: `A HUNDRED DEAR, A HUNDRED SORROWS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love, and feel how dear they are. If an edge of fear comes with it, that they might be hurt, or leave, or die, notice it gently; that's the sorrow the Buddha was counting. Don't push the love away; just loosen your grip a little, the way you'd hold a bird: close enough to keep it warm, open enough to let it breathe.
Soka, sorrow. The Buddha's words to the grieving Visakha: a hundred dear ones, a hundred sorrows; one dear, one sorrow. Today's word.
Your line: with an open hand. The Buddha let Visakha do the arithmetic herself. Day six hundred twenty-two, done.

623.title: There is an unborn
623.hook: there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade; were there not, there'd be no escape
623.carry: because there is, an escape is known
623.howItsDone: The saying on the unborn is studied in Theravada teaching on nibbana and is quoted by teachers of many Buddhist schools; it also appears in the Itivuttaka (Iti 43).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Visakha's wet hair at midday. Your line: with an open hand. Today closes a week, with a short saying about what isn't made.

Everything you've ever touched was born, or made, or put together. Your phone. Your house. Your body. Your mood this morning. Every one of them came from causes, and every one will come apart. That raises a hard question. If everything is made, and everything comes apart, is there anything at all that isn't? Is there a way out of the making? In the eighth and last chapter of the Udana, the Buddha answers with four words that start with un.
screen: `EVERYTHING YOU'VE TOUCHED WAS MADE.` → `EVERYTHING MADE COMES APART.` → `IS THERE A WAY OUT?`

segments.voice: The setting is a talk on nibbana to the monks. Here's the saying, paraphrased closely. There is, monks, an unborn, an unbecome, an unmade, an unconditioned. If there were not this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, no escape would be known from the born, the become, the made, the conditioned. But because there is, an escape is known. Notice where the weight falls: on two small words, there is. Not it might be, not we hope. The text doesn't describe the unborn at all. It argues for it, from the escape: if there were only the made, there'd be no way out of it. How do traditions read it? Theravada teachers generally read the unborn as nibbana itself: not a self, not a soul, not a creator, but the unconditioned. Other schools have drawn on the passage in their own ways. The text itself simply says, there is. Look back at the week. Nanda's pull home. Meghiya not yet ripe. The elephant read whole. Moths at the lamp. Suppavasa giving. Visakha's hundred sorrows. Every one was about the born and the made. Today, the Udana points past them.
screen: `A TALK ON NIBBANA.` · `UNBORN, UNBECOME, UNMADE.` · `IF THERE WERE NOT, NO ESCAPE.` · `IT SAYS WHAT IT ISN'T.` · then, large: `THERE IS AN UNBORN.`

segments.voice: Notice how everything in your experience is moving: the breath, sounds, sensations, thoughts arriving and leaving. Don't chase any of them, and don't try to find the unborn either; it isn't a thing to find. Let the movement go on, and rest as the quiet that notices it.
Ajāta. Unborn: one of four words, with unbecome, unmade and unconditioned, that the Udana uses for nibbana, the escape from everything made.
Your line: because there is, an escape is known. A week of the born and the made, and one saying that points past them. That's a week.
